Notes on Shelf Runs

A shelf run that looks tidy on the floor plan is often the one that fails the access check, because the plan does not show the turning circle the trolley needs behind the end panel. Leave at least ten times the trolley width of clearance at every aisle head, and set the overflow into the bay rather than stacking it on the floor, since a floor stack turns a reading room into a trip hazard nobody planned for.

Shelf loading is the other quiet killer. Once you exceed the rated load the uprights inside the bay bow a little, and a bowed upright drops books that no shelf read will find. A second pair of hands and a spare trolley cost less than restocking a run after the fact.

Label both ends before the move, not after. Spine labels written with a pigment pen survive the handling; adhesive strips do not, and an unlabelled run in a full bay is effectively a new run the next time anyone has to trace it, which is the most expensive kind of shortcut there is.

Finally, photograph every bay before the covers go back on. The photograph is the only shelf-order record that stays accurate, and it costs nothing compared with a full stock count later to find out whether the reserve sequence was ever reshelved into the north wall at all.
